We then extend the study to a full large language model, showing how fine-tuning on various collections of natural language prompts can elicit similar in-context and in-weight learning behaviour.

papers.title: A Simple Generalisation of the Implicit Dynamics of In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning work in transformers? Specifically, can the implicit weight update result be generalized to all tokens, any block, and more realistic transformer blocks with layer normalization?
papers.core_contribution: The paper generalizes the implicit weight update result for in-context learning to all sequence positions, any transformer block, and more realistic residual blocks including layer normalization.
papers.conclusion: The results help to bring the theory of implicit dynamics in ICL closer to practice, with potential for validation on large-scale models.
papers.key_findings:
The implicit weight update for any token and any block is a rank-one update, as shown in Theorem 1.
The theoretical predictions match empirical results on in-context linear regression tasks.
The alignment of implicit weight updates across tokens shows consistent structure across blocks.
The alignment of weight updates for the last token across blocks does not show a particular structure.
papers.limitation: The work is limited to one step of token generation and does not consider ICL settings where the answer is a sequence of tokens.
future_direction: Analyze the implicit weight updates of models trained on language.
Study ICL settings where the answer is a sequence of tokens.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) refers to the ability of a model to learn new tasks from examples in its input without any parameter updates. In contrast to previous theories of ICL relying on toy models and data settings, recently it has been shown that an abstraction of a transformer block can be seen as implicitly updating the weights of its feedforward network according to the context (Dherin et al., 2025). Here, we provide a simple generalisation of this result for (i) all sequence positions beyond the last, (ii) any transformer block beyond the first, and (iii) more realistic residual blocks including layer normalisation. We empirically verify our theory on simple in-context linear regression tasks and investigate the relationship between the implicit updates related to different tokens within and between blocks. These results help to bring the theory of Dherin et al. (2025) even closer to practice, with potential for validation on large-scale models.

papers.title: Understanding Verbatim Memorization in LLMs Through Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: What specific circuits in the model are responsible for initiating and maintaining verbatim memorization, and how do they differ from non-memorized generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrastive datasets and circuit discovery to identify circuits responsible for memorization in LLMs, finding that initiation circuits can also maintain memorization, but maintenance circuits cannot initiate it, and that memorization prevention transfers across domains while induction is context-dependent.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that memorization initiation and maintenance are handled by different circuits, with initiation circuits being more general and maintenance circuits being more specific. Memorization prevention transfers across domains, while induction is context-dependent.
papers.key_findings:
Created two distinct contrastive datasets for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks.
Discovered compact circuits (≤5% of model edges) for memorization decision and branch comparison tasks using attribution patching techniques.
Circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.
Memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains (GitHub, Enron Emails, Common Crawl), while memorization induction appears more context-dependent.
Removing memorization (noising approach) is easier than inducing memorization (denoising approach) in the studied setup.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG) for circuit discovery, which provides only an approximation and may not fully correlate with direct activation patching measurements.
Findings are limited to a single, relatively small language model (GPT-Neo-125m); larger models might employ more complex or differently distributed memorization mechanisms.
Uncertainty about whether the identified circuits represent general memorization mechanisms or are specific to the Wikipedia subset of The Pile or artifacts of the contrastive dataset construction.
future_direction: Investigate how memorization mechanisms scale with model size.
Explore whether similar circuits exist in different model architectures.
Expand testing to more diverse datasets and memorization criteria to establish the generality of these mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Underlying mechanisms of memorization in LLMs-the verbatim reproduction of training data-remain poorly understood.What exact part of the network decides to retrieve a token that we would consider as start of memorization sequence?How exactly is the models' behaviour different when producing memorized sentence vs non-memorized?In this work we approach these questions from mechanistic interpretability standpoint by utilizing transformer circuits-the minimal computational subgraphs that perform specific functions within the model.Through carefully constructed contrastive datasets, we identify points where model generation diverges from memorized content and isolate the specific circuits responsible for two distinct aspects of memorization.We find that circuits that initiate memorization can also maintain it once started, while circuits that only maintain memorization cannot trigger its initiation.Intriguingly, memorization prevention mechanisms transfer robustly across different text domains, while memorization induction appears more contextdependent. 1

papers.title: LLM Agents Display Human Biases but Exhibit Distinct Learning Patterns
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit human-like behavioral biases in Decisions from Experience tasks and how their learning patterns differ from humans.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs display human biases on aggregate but exhibit distinct learning patterns due to strong recency bias, lacking phenomena like 'surprise triggers change' and 'wavy recency effect' observed in humans.
papers.conclusion: LLMs appear human-like on aggregate in DFE tasks, but detailed analysis reveals different underlying processes due to recency bias, emphasizing the need for careful investigation when using LLMs to simulate human behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs and humans both exhibit underweighting of rare events, but LLMs do so more extremely.
Both LLMs and humans show the correlation effect, but humans learn faster except for the Gemini-all model.
LLMs exhibit a strong recency bias, considering only the most recent outcomes, unlike humans who consider a larger window.
Humans robustly show the wavy recency effect and surprise triggers change, which are entirely absent in LLMs.
LLMs' choice patterns closely match the Recency Player strategy, indicating a reliance on recent feedback.
future_direction: Asking models to portray a specific persona or predict human choices in DFE tasks.
Fine-tuning LLMs to experience-related decision tasks to make patterns more comparable to humans.
Expanding the scope of research to more models and decision scenarios.
papers.abstract: We investigate the choice patterns of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the context of Decisions from Experience tasks that involve repeated choice and learning from feedback, and compare their behavior to human participants. We find that on the aggregate, LLMs appear to display behavioral biases similar to humans: both exhibit underweighting rare events and correlation effects. However, more nuanced analyses of the choice patterns reveal that this happens for very different reasons. LLMs exhibit strong recency biases, unlike humans, who appear to respond in more sophisticated ways. While these different processes may lead to similar behavior on average, choice patterns contingent on recent events differ vastly between the two groups. Specifically, phenomena such as ``surprise triggers change" and the ``wavy recency effect of rare events" are robustly observed in humans, but entirely absent in LLMs. Our findings provide insights into the limitations of using LLMs to simulate and predict humans in learning environments and highlight the need for refined analyses of their behavior when investigating whether they replicate human decision making tendencies.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Identifying and Manipulating Personality Traits in LLMs Through Activation Engineering
papers.research_question: How can personality traits in large language models be identified and manipulated using activation engineering to enable dynamic personality adjustment without extensive retraining?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces 'feature induction', a method for identifying and manipulating personality traits in LLMs through activation engineering, enabling dynamic personality customization without extensive retraining.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that activation engineering can be used to identify and manipulate personality traits in LLMs, enabling dynamic customization without retraining, while highlighting ethical implications.
papers.key_findings:
Layer 18 in Llama 3 8B is the most influential layer for personality trait expression.
Personality traits can be clustered into meaningful groups based on activation vectors, revealing semantic relationships.
Principal component analysis identifies key personality dimensions and traits that capture most variance.
Socially undesirable personality traits are grouped together in activation space, with proximal traits like competitive and confident.
An interactive interface allows real-time control of LLM personality by adjusting principal component weights.
future_direction: Enhancing interpretability by mapping personality traits to specific layer activations and neurons.
Analyzing the performance consequences of different personality factors on LLM competencies.
Extending the research to multilingual models to understand cultural specificity of personality traits.
papers.abstract: The field of large language models (LLMs) has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by the desire for better efficiency, interpretability, and safe use. Building on the novel approach of "activation engineering," this study explores personality modification in LLMs, drawing inspiration from research like Refusal in LLMs Is Mediated by a Single Direction (arXiv:2406.11717) and Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition (arXiv:2312.06681). We leverage activation engineering to develop a method for identifying and adjusting activation directions related to personality traits, which may allow for dynamic LLM personality fine-tuning. This work aims to further our understanding of LLM interpretability while examining the ethical implications of such developments.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify directions in activation space (persona vectors) underlying personality traits in language models, and use them to monitor and control persona shifts during deployment and finetuning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an automated pipeline to extract persona vectors from natural language descriptions, and demonstrates that these vectors can be used to monitor and control persona shifts in language models during deployment and finetuning.
papers.conclusion: Persona vectors provide a powerful framework for understanding and controlling personality shifts in large language models, with applications in monitoring, mitigation, and prevention of undesirable trait expression.
papers.key_findings:
Persona vectors can be extracted automatically and used to control trait expression via steering and to monitor prompt-induced behavioral shifts.
Finetuning-induced persona shifts are strongly correlated with activation changes along the corresponding persona vectors.
Post-hoc steering can mitigate unwanted persona shifts after finetuning, but may degrade general capabilities.
Preventative steering during finetuning can limit persona shifts while better preserving general capabilities.
Projection of training data onto persona vectors can predict persona shifts before finetuning, enabling data filtering.
papers.limitation:
Persona vectors are effective for detecting clear prompt-induced shifts but may be less reliable for more subtle behavioral changes in deployment settings.
Steering interventions can introduce side effects and degrade model performance on general capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models interact with users through a simulated 'Assistant' persona. While the Assistant is typically trained to be helpful, harmless, and honest, it sometimes deviates from these ideals. In this paper, we identify directions in the model's activation space-persona vectors-underlying several traits, such as evil, sycophancy, and propensity to hallucinate. We confirm that these vectors can be used to monitor fluctuations in the Assistant's personality at deployment time. We then apply persona vectors to predict and control personality shifts that occur during training. We find that both intended and unintended personality changes after finetuning are strongly correlated with shifts along the relevant persona vectors. These shifts can be mitigated through post-hoc intervention, or avoided in the first place with a new preventative steering method. Moreover, persona vectors can be used to flag training data that will produce undesirable personality changes, both at the dataset level and the individual sample level. Our method for extracting persona vectors is automated and can be applied to any personality trait of interest, given only a natural-language description.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: PERSONA: Dynamic and Compositional Inference-Time Personality Control via Activation Vector Algebra
papers.research_question: How can we achieve dynamic and compositional personality control in Large Language Models without fine-tuning, by directly manipulating personality vectors in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PERSONA, a training-free framework for dynamic and compositional personality control in LLMs via activation vector algebra, achieving fine-tuning level performance by extracting and manipulating orthogonal personality vectors in the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: Personality control in LLMs can be achieved through activation vector algebra, providing evidence that aspects of LLM personality are mathematically tractable and opening new directions for interpretable and efficient behavioral control.
papers.key_findings:
Personality traits can be represented as approximately orthogonal, extractable vectors in the model's activation space via contrastive analysis.
These personality vectors support algebraic operations (scalar multiplication, addition, subtraction) for precise and compositional control of trait intensity and combination.
The PERSONA framework achieves a mean score of 9.60 on PersonalityBench, nearly matching the supervised fine-tuning upper bound of 9.61, and up to 91% win rates on the dynamic PERSONA-EVOLVE benchmark.
papers.abstract: Current methods for personality control in Large Language Models rely on static prompting or expensive fine-tuning, failing to capture the dynamic and compositional nature of human traits. We introduce PERSONA, a training-free framework that achieves fine-tuning level performance through direct manipulation of personality vectors in activation space. Our key insight is that personality traits appear as extractable, approximately orthogonal directions in the model's representation space that support algebraic operations. The framework operates through three stages: Persona-Base extracts orthogonal trait vectors via contrastive activation analysis; Persona-Algebra enables precise control through vector arithmetic (scalar multiplication for intensity, addition for composition, subtraction for suppression); and Persona-Flow achieves context-aware adaptation by dynamically composing these vectors during inference. On PersonalityBench, our approach achieves a mean score of 9.60, nearly matching the supervised fine-tuning upper bound of 9.61 without any gradient updates. On our proposed Persona-Evolve benchmark for dynamic personality adaptation, we achieve up to 91% win rates across diverse model families. These results provide evidence that aspects of LLM personality are mathematically tractable, opening new directions for interpretable and efficient behavioral control.

papers.title: Unveiling the Latent Directions of Reflection in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we systematically identify effective trigger instructions for reflection, and do these instructions correspond to latent directions in the model's hidden space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using activation steering to identify latent directions of reflection in LLMs, enabling systematic discovery of reflection-inducing instructions and control over reflective behavior, with the finding that suppressing reflection is easier than enhancing it.
papers.conclusion: The findings provide initial evidence that reflection corresponds to consistent activation patterns, paving the way for future interpretability work, and highlight a dual-use concern where steering can enhance reflection as a defense mechanism but also be exploited to inhibit reflection for jailbreaks.
papers.key_findings:
Reflection levels (no, intrinsic, triggered) show clear stratification in model accuracy.
Steering vectors can discover new reflection-inducing instructions beyond known ones.
Reflection can be enhanced or inhibited via activation interventions at inference time.
Suppressing reflection is easier than inducing it.
Latent directions of reflection are more faithfully captured by steering vectors than by surface-level embedding similarity.
papers.limitation:
The method provides a broad overview of reflection in activations but does not drill down into specific components like attention heads or MLP neurons.
Experiments are limited to two small-sized models (Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT) and two datasets.
Theoretical understanding is limited; accuracy does not vary linearly with latent directions, requiring deeper treatment.
future_direction: Applying fine-grained approaches like activation patching, causal tracing, or circuit analysis to pinpoint precise circuits responsible for reflection.
Investigating whether the model internally maintains a form of 'consistency score' or probability mass over coherent reasoning trajectories.
Expanding evaluation to larger LLMs, different architectures, or broader datasets (e.g., MATH, HumanEval).
papers.abstract: Reflection, the ability of large language models (LLMs) to evaluate and revise their own reasoning, has been widely used to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks. Yet, most prior works emphasizes designing reflective prompting strategies or reinforcement learning objectives, leaving the inner mechanisms of reflection underexplored. In this paper, we investigate reflection through the lens of latent directions in model activations. We propose a methodology based on activation steering to characterize how instructions with different reflective intentions: no reflection, intrinsic reflection, and triggered reflection. By constructing steering vectors between these reflection levels, we demonstrate that (1) new reflection-inducing instructions can be systematically identified, (2) reflective behavior can be directly enhanced or suppressed through activation interventions, and (3) suppressing reflection is considerably easier than stimulating it. Experiments on GSM8k-adv and Cruxeval-o-adv with Qwen2.5-3B and Gemma3-4B-IT reveal clear stratification across reflection levels, and steering interventions confirm the controllability of reflection. Our findings highlight both opportunities (e.g., reflection-enhancing defenses) and risks (e.g., adversarial inhibition of reflection in jailbreak attacks). This work opens a path toward mechanistic understanding of reflective reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Spurious Rewards Paradox: Mechanistically Understanding How RLVR Activates Memorization Shortcuts in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does spurious reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) activate memorization shortcuts in large language models, leading to improved accuracy on contaminated data despite incorrect rewards?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers an Anchor-Adapter circuit in Qwen models that explains how spurious RLVR triggers memorization shortcuts, leading to a Perplexity Paradox where answer perplexity decreases while prompt perplexity increases, and demonstrates causal steering via MLP interventions.
papers.conclusion: Our work demonstrates that reinforcement learning can inadvertently trigger shortcuts by activating latent memorized data rather than fostering genuine reasoning, providing tools to distinguish between appearance of capability and genuine generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Spurious RLVR leads to a Perplexity Paradox: answer token perplexity decreases while prompt perplexity increases, indicating memorization shortcuts.
A Functional Anchor in layers 18-20 triggers retrieval of memorized answers, while Structural Adapters in layers 21+ transform representations to accommodate the shortcut.
Neural Differential Equations show a bifurcation in the latent space trajectories between memorized and reasoned samples, with separation force peaking at the anchor layers.
Ablation studies confirm that the anchor layers are necessary for memorization on contaminated data, while stable reasoning remains unaffected.
Mechanistic intervention by scaling specific MLP keys allows bidirectional steering of the model's reliance on contaminated data.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) is highly effective for enhancing LLM reasoning, yet recent evidence shows models like Qwen 2.5 achieve significant gains even with spurious or incorrect rewards. We investigate this phenomenon and identify a "Perplexity Paradox": spurious RLVR triggers a divergence where answer-token perplexity drops while prompt-side coherence degrades, suggesting the model is bypassing reasoning in favor of memorization. Using Path Patching, Logit Lens, JSD analysis, and Neural Differential Equations, we uncover a hidden Anchor-Adapter circuit that facilitates this shortcut. We localize a Functional Anchor in the middle layers (L18-20) that triggers the retrieval of memorized solutions, followed by Structural Adapters in later layers (L21+) that transform representations to accommodate the shortcut signal. Finally, we demonstrate that scaling specific MLP keys within this circuit allows for bidirectional causal steering-artificially amplifying or suppressing contamination-driven performance. Our results provide a mechanistic roadmap for identifying and mitigating data contamination in RLVR-tuned models. Code is available at https://github.com/idwts/How-RLVR-Activates-Memorization-Shortcuts.

papers.title: Language Models Are Capable of Metacognitive Monitoring and Control of Their Internal Activations
papers.research_question: Can LLMs accurately monitor and control their internal neural activations? Why can they report some intermediate steps but not others?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a neurofeedback paradigm to quantify metacognitive abilities in LLMs, showing they can report and control internal activations along certain axes, with performance depending on interpretability, variance, and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have limited metacognitive abilities to monitor and control their internal activations, which raises important considerations for AI safety and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can report neural activations along target axes, with performance improving with more in-context examples and being better for semantically interpretable axes.
LLMs can explicitly and implicitly control neural activations, with explicit control being stronger and effects increasing with model size and depth.
Control effects are stronger for axes with semantic interpretability and those explaining more variance.
The axes that can be reported and controlled span a low-dimensional 'metacognitive space'.
Metacognitive abilities have implications for AI safety, as models might evade neural-based oversight.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to instruction-fine-tuned models and may not generalize to base models.
The neurofeedback paradigm assumes the model can understand the task, which may not hold for all models or tasks.
future_direction: Extend the neurofeedback paradigm to more models and datasets.
Investigate the neural mechanisms underlying metacognitive control in LLMs.
Explore applications in AI safety, such as developing better oversight methods.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can sometimes report the strategies they actually use to solve tasks, yet at other times seem unable to recognize those strategies that govern their behavior. This suggests a limited degree of metacognition - the capacity to monitor one's own cognitive processes for subsequent reporting and self-control. Metacognition enhances LLMs' capabilities in solving complex tasks but also raises safety concerns, as models may obfuscate their internal processes to evade neural-activation-based oversight (e.g., safety detector). Given society's increased reliance on these models, it is critical that we understand their metacognitive abilities. To address this, we introduce a neuroscience-inspired neurofeedback paradigm that uses in-context learning to quantify metacognitive abilities of LLMs to report and control their activation patterns. We demonstrate that their abilities depend on several factors: the number of in-context examples provided, the semantic interpretability of the neural activation direction (to be reported/controlled), and the variance explained by that direction. These directions span a "metacognitive space" with dimensionality much lower than the model's neural space, suggesting LLMs can monitor only a small subset of their neural activations. Our paradigm provides empirical evidence to quantify metacognition in LLMs, with significant implications for AI safety (e.g., adversarial attack and defense).

papers.title: Do Natural Language Descriptions of Model Activations Convey Privileged Information?
papers.research_question: Do natural language descriptions of model activations (verbalization) provide privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, or do they mainly convey input information and the verbalizer's own knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that existing verbalization methods often do not convey privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, but instead reflect input information or the verbalizer's own knowledge, highlighting the need for better benchmarks and controls.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
For feature extraction datasets, a zero-shot baseline achieves high accuracy without access to activations, suggesting privileged knowledge may not be necessary for verbalization to succeed.
Prediction on reconstructed text (via inversion) matches verbalization performance, indicating tasks may elicit input text information rather than privileged knowledge.
Verbalizers often rely on their own world knowledge, especially when there is a mismatch between target and verbalizer knowledge, as shown in PersonaQA experiments.
Verbalization is sensitive to prompt phrasing, complicating interpretation of verbalizer outputs.
future_direction: Developing better benchmarks and experimental controls to assess verbalization methods.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability methods have proposed to translate LLM internal representations into natural language descriptions using a second verbalizer LLM. This is intended to illuminate how the target model represents and operates on inputs. But do such activation verbalization approaches actually provide privileged knowledge about the internal workings of the target model, or do they merely convey information about its inputs? We critically evaluate popular verbalization methods across datasets used in prior work and find that they can succeed at benchmarks without any access to target model internals, suggesting that these datasets may not be ideal for evaluating verbalization methods. We then run controlled experiments which reveal that verbalizations often reflect the parametric knowledge of the verbalizer LLM which generated them, rather than the knowledge of the target LLM whose activations are decoded. Taken together, our results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.

papers.title: Indications of Belief-Guided Agency and Meta-Cognitive Monitoring in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the behavior of large language models indicate belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring as defined by the HOT-3 indicator for consciousness?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework and the Belief Dominance metric to test the HOT-3 indicator in LLMs, providing empirical evidence for belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates the existence of agency guided by a general belief formation and action selection system regulated by meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs, contributing to the study of AI consciousness.
papers.key_findings:
External manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation.
Belief formation causally drives the model's action selection.
Models can monitor and report their own belief states, indicating meta-cognitive monitoring.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic implementation of belief formation, action selection, and meta-cognition remains unclear.
The framework is restricted to capturing beliefs that can be expressed in words.
The framework currently only tests two competing beliefs.
future_direction: Studying the mechanistic implementation of belief formation and meta-cognitive monitoring.
Extending the framework to capture latent beliefs beyond existing vocabulary.
Testing additional consciousness criteria in more capable models.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) have sparked the question whether these models possess some form of consciousness. To tackle this challenge, Butlin et al. (2023) introduced a list of indicators for consciousness in artificial systems based on neuroscientific theories. In this work, we evaluate a key indicator from this list, called HOT-3, which tests for agency guided by a general belief-formation and action selection system that updates beliefs based on meta-cognitive monitoring. We view beliefs as representations in the model's latent space that emerge in response to a given input, and introduce a metric to quantify their dominance during generation. Analyzing the dynamics between competing beliefs across models and tasks reveals three key findings: (1) external manipulations systematically modulate internal belief formation, (2) belief formation causally drives the model's action selection, and (3) models can monitor and report their own belief states. Together, these results provide empirical support for the existence of belief-guided agency and meta-cognitive monitoring in LLMs. More broadly, our work lays methodological groundwork for investigating the emergence of agency, beliefs, and meta-cognition in LLMs.

papers.title: How do language models learn facts? Dynamics, curricula and hallucinations
papers.research_question: How do language models acquire factual knowledge during training, and what are the dynamics, the impact of data distribution, and the challenges of integrating new knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a three-phase learning process for factual recall in language models, shows how data distribution affects dynamics, and demonstrates that fine-tuning to add new knowledge is challenging due to hallucinations and corruption of existing memories.
papers.conclusion: The paper emphasizes the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggests data scheduling strategies to accelerate training, while highlighting the difficulty of integrating new knowledge post-training.
papers.key_findings:
Language models learn factual recall in three phases: initial language understanding, a performance plateau, and then knowledge emergence.
The plateau phase corresponds to the development of attention-based recall circuits.
Imbalanced data distributions shorten the plateau but can lead to overfitting.
Hallucinations (overconfident predictions on unseen individuals) emerge simultaneously with knowledge acquisition.
Fine-tuning to incorporate new knowledge quickly corrupts existing parametric memories.
papers.limitation: The results do not rule out that other qualitative changes may occur during the plateau phase, and they do not provide any mechanistic insights regarding how models acquire individual-specific knowledge.
future_direction: Further investigation is needed to better understand the precise conditions under which data repetition can effectively reduce time spent on performance plateaus during training.
The data scheduling strategy could be dynamically adjusted based on observed plateau termination.
papers.abstract: Large language models accumulate vast knowledge during pre-training, yet the dynamics governing this acquisition remain poorly understood. This work investigates the learning dynamics of language models on a synthetic factual recall task, uncovering three key findings: First, language models learn in three phases, exhibiting a performance plateau before acquiring precise factual knowledge. Mechanistically, this plateau coincides with the formation of attention-based circuits that support recall. Second, the training data distribution significantly impacts learning dynamics, as imbalanced distributions lead to shorter plateaus. Finally, hallucinations emerge simultaneously with knowledge, and integrating new knowledge into the model through fine-tuning is challenging, as it quickly corrupts its existing parametric memories. Our results emphasize the importance of data distribution in knowledge acquisition and suggest novel data scheduling strategies to accelerate neural network training.

papers.title: How Does Controllability Emerge In Language Models During Pretraining?
papers.research_question: How does linear steerability emerge in language models during pretraining, and why does it vary across concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Linear steerability emerges during intermediate stages of training, varies across concepts, and is linked to increasing linear separability of concepts in the hidden space.
papers.conclusion: Linear steerability does not emerge uniformly but develops over training and varies between concepts, aligning with increasingly structured internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Linear steerability emerges in later training stages, separate from reasoning capability and emotion expression via prompting.
Emergence times vary widely across concepts, such as anger emerging earlier than sadness.
Concept representations become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses.
The Intervention Detector (ID) framework can reveal steerability dynamics and predict when linear steerability emerges.
These findings hold across different model families, indicating a general pattern.
papers.limitation:
Only evaluated on 7B-scale open-source models, not tested on larger LLMs.
Intervention coefficient was empirically tuned and differs across models, with underlying causes not investigated.
Did not explore alternative nonlinear approaches for extracting or intervening in model representations.
Methodological innovation in intervention techniques is not the focus; core procedure is consistent with prior work.
Alternative unsupervised methods such as mean-difference vectors are not compared.
Concepts like emotions lack ground truth, making evaluation subjective and based on semantic interpretation.
Steering certain concepts can produce offensive outputs, with no safety filtering applied.
future_direction: Examining how different pre-training corpora influence intervention outcomes.
Exploring alternative steering methods beyond PCA or K-Means.
Comparing unsupervised methods like mean-difference vectors and their influence on downstream intervention performance.
papers.abstract: Language models can be steered by modifying their internal representations to control concepts such as emotion, style, or truthfulness in generation. However, the conditions for an effective intervention remain unclear and are often validated through heuristics and trial-and-error. To fill this gap, we demonstrate that intervention efficacy, measured by linear steerability (i.e., the ability to adjust output via linear transformations of hidden states), emerges during intermediate stages of training. Moreover, even closely related concepts (e.g., anger and sadness) exhibit steerability emergence at distinct stages of training. To better interpret the dynamics of steerability during training, we adapt existing intervention techniques into a unified framework, referred to as the "Intervention Detector" (ID), which is designed to reveal how linear steerability evolves over the course of training through hidden state and representation analysis. ID reveals that concepts become increasingly linearly separable in the hidden space as training progresses, which strongly correlates with the emergence of linear steerability. We further introduce ID-based metrics, such as heatmaps, entropy trends, and cosine similarity, to help interpret how linear steerability evolves throughout training. In addition, we apply ID across different model families to ensure the generality of our findings on steerability dynamics.

papers.title: Enhancing Multiple Dimensions of Trustworthiness in LLMs via Sparse Activation Control
papers.research_question: How can we enhance multiple dimensions of trustworthiness (safety, factuality, bias) in LLMs simultaneously without training, by controlling sparse activations in specific model components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Sparse Activation Control, a training-free method that enhances multiple trustworthiness dimensions in LLMs by identifying sparse, task-specific attention heads and controlling their representations using Gaussian Mixture Models, avoiding control conflicts.
papers.conclusion: Sparse Activation Control is an effective training-free method for enhancing multi-dimensional trustworthiness in LLMs by leveraging sparse and independent task-specific components.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse Activation Control can enhance safety, factuality, and bias simultaneously without significant interference, outperforming representation engineering baselines in multi-task control.
Attention heads for different tasks are sparse and have minimal overlap, allowing independent control.
The method does not significantly harm general model performance on MMLU and CSQA.
The method generalizes to other models (Qwen series) and additional trustworthiness tasks (robustness, privacy).
Control shifts head outputs towards task-relevant tokens, as shown by unembedding projections.
papers.limitation:
Relies on construction of paired stimuli, which may require domain knowledge.
Experiments are limited to a few models and tasks.
future_direction: Extend to more tasks and models
Explore theoretical foundations of sparsity
papers.abstract: As the development and application of Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance rapidly, enhancing their trustworthiness and aligning them with human preferences has become a critical area of research. Traditional methods rely heavily on extensive data for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), but representation engineering offers a new, training-free approach. This technique leverages semantic features to control the representation of LLM's intermediate hidden states, enabling the model to meet specific requirements such as increased honesty or heightened safety awareness. However, a significant challenge arises when attempting to fulfill multiple requirements simultaneously. It proves difficult to encode various semantic contents, like honesty and safety, into a singular semantic feature, restricting its practicality. In this work, we address this issue through ``Sparse Activation Control''. By delving into the intrinsic mechanisms of LLMs, we manage to identify and pinpoint components that are closely related to specific tasks within the model, i.e., attention heads. These heads display sparse characteristics that allow for near-independent control over different tasks. Our experiments, conducted on the open-source Llama series models, have yielded encouraging results. The models were able to align with human preferences on issues of safety, factuality, and bias concurrently.

papers.title: MLPs Learn In-Context on Regression and Classification Tasks
papers.research_question: Can multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) learn in-context, and how does their performance compare to Transformers on synthetic in-context learning and relational reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: MLPs can learn in-context on synthetic regression and classification tasks comparably to Transformers under the same compute budget, and outperform Transformers on classical relational reasoning tasks, challenging prior assumptions about their capabilities.
papers.conclusion: MLPs are capable of in-context learning and relational reasoning, challenging prior arguments against their ability, and encouraging further study of MLP architectures in more complex settings to understand the comparative advantage of attention-based schemes.
papers.key_findings:
MLPs can learn in-context on regression and classification tasks.
MLPs perform comparably to Transformers on ICL tasks under the same compute budget.
MLPs outperform Transformers on relational reasoning tasks (match-to-sample, sphere oddball, line oddball).
MLPs exhibit a transition from in-weight learning to in-context learning as data diversity increases, similar to Transformers.
Vanilla MLPs struggle with long context lengths in ICL regression, but MLP-Mixers do not.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear how MLPs perform against Transformers at scale on real-world tasks, and where a performance gap may originate.
future_direction: Further exploration of MLP architectures in more complex settings to better understand the potential comparative advantage of attention-based schemes.
papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL), the remarkable ability to solve a task from only input exemplars, is often assumed to be a unique hallmark of Transformer models. By examining commonly employed synthetic ICL tasks, we demonstrate that multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) can also learn in-context. Moreover, MLPs, and the closely related MLP-Mixer models, learn in-context comparably with Transformers under the same compute budget in this setting. We further show that MLPs outperform Transformers on a series of classical tasks from psychology designed to test relational reasoning, which are closely related to in-context classification. These results underscore a need for studying in-context learning beyond attention-based architectures, while also challenging prior arguments against MLPs' ability to solve relational tasks. Altogether, our results highlight the unexpected competence of MLPs in a synthetic setting, and support the growing interest in all-MLP alternatives to Transformer architectures. It remains unclear how MLPs perform against Transformers at scale on real-world tasks, and where a performance gap may originate. We encourage further exploration of these architectures in more complex settings to better understand the potential comparative advantage of attention-based schemes.

papers.title: Generating Diverse Translation by Manipulating Multi-Head Attention
papers.research_question: The paper investigates how different attention heads in Transformer's encoder-decoder multi-head attention align to different translation candidates and proposes a method to generate diverse translations by manipulating these heads.
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that different attention heads in Transformer's encoder-decoder attention align to different translation candidates and proposes a method to generate diverse translations by selectively sampling these heads, improving diversity without severe quality loss.
papers.conclusion: The paper discovers an internal characteristic of Transformer multi-head attention and uses it to generate diverse translations, with applications in back-translation and conversation response generation showing significant improvements.
papers.key_findings:
Different attention heads in the final decoder layer align to different source word translation candidates.
By manipulating these heads, diverse translations can be generated without a severe drop in quality.
The proposed method outperforms previous diversity-enhancing methods in translation tasks.
Using diverse translations for back-translation improves machine translation performance.
The method also enhances diversity in conversation response generation tasks.
papers.abstract: Transformer model has been widely used on machine translation tasks and obtained state-of-the-art results. In this paper, we report an interesting phenomenon in its encoder-decoder multi-head attention: different attention heads of the final decoder layer align to different word translation candidates. We empirically verify this discovery and propose a method to generate diverse translations by manipulating heads. Furthermore, we make use of these diverse translations with the back-translation technique for better data augmentation. Experiment results show that our method generates diverse translations without severe drop in translation quality. Experiments also show that back-translation with these diverse translations could bring significant improvement on performance on translation tasks. An auxiliary experiment of conversation response generation task proves the effect of diversity as well.

papers.title: Meta-Learning Neural Mechanisms rather than Bayesian Priors
papers.research_question: What does meta-learning imbue models with? Does it learn simplicity-based priors or neural mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Meta-training imprints neural mechanisms (e.g., counters) into models, rather than learning simplicity-based priors, providing efficient meta-learning paradigms and theoretical insights linking symbolic theories and neural mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: Meta-trained models do not mimic the statistical properties of their meta-training dataset; instead, they acquire useful neural mechanisms, and meta-training on mechanistically-complex languages is vital for encouraging such mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Models meta-trained on simplicity-bias datasets do not outperform those on complexity-bias datasets, contradicting the simplicity-bias view.
Meta-training on a single formal language can be as effective as meta-training on 5000 different languages if the language incentivizes useful neural mechanisms.
Meta-training on context-free and context-sensitive languages outperforms meta-training on regular languages, indicating mechanistic complexity matters.
GRUs do not show the same meta-learning improvement as LSTMs, likely because they cannot acquire counting mechanisms.
The Chomsky hierarchy may not fully capture the neural mechanisms useful for a given architecture, suggesting need for alternative hierarchies.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to formal language learning and does not look at more complicated domains like natural language.
The work does not explicitly examine hidden layers to find the presence of neural counters.
future_direction: Investigate alternative theoretical hierarchies that correspond to neural mechanisms useful in specific architectures.
Explore meta-learning in different architectures beyond LSTMs and GRUs, such as Transformers or Stack-RNNs.
Develop computational hierarchies akin to the Chomsky hierarchy but defined in terms of neural architectures and their mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Children acquire language despite being exposed to several orders of magnitude less data than large language models require. Meta-learning has been proposed as a way to integrate human-like learning biases into neural-network architectures, combining both the structured generalizations of symbolic models with the scalability of neural-network models. But what does meta-learning exactly imbue the model with? We investigate the meta-learning of formal languages and find that, contrary to previous claims, meta-trained models are not learning simplicity-based priors when meta-trained on datasets organised around simplicity. Rather, we find evidence that meta-training imprints neural mechanisms (such as counters) into the model, which function like cognitive primitives for the network on downstream tasks. Most surprisingly, we find that meta-training on a single formal language can provide as much improvement to a model as meta-training on 5000 different formal languages, provided that the formal language incentivizes the learning of useful neural mechanisms. Taken together, our findings provide practical implications for efficient meta-learning paradigms and new theoretical insights into linking symbolic theories and neural mechanisms.

papers.title: Do LLMs Know about Hallucination? An Empirical Investigation of LLM's Hidden States
papers.research_question: Do LLMs possess awareness of hallucination, and if so, to what extent and through what mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Provides empirical evidence that LLMs exhibit awareness of hallucination through differences in hidden states when processing correct vs hallucinated answers, and shows potential for using hidden state guidance to mitigate hallucination.
papers.conclusion: LLMs possess awareness of hallucination as evidenced by differences in hidden states, and leveraging hidden state guidance can help mitigate hallucination.
papers.key_findings:
LLM’s final hidden state is more susceptible to be influenced by a correct answer compared to a hallucinated one.
Strategically inducing an LLM to produce hallucinated responses can raise its awareness consequently.
The level of awareness corresponds to the uncertainty of the LLM in the responses.
Providing relevant knowledge can assist LLMs in identifying hallucinated responses.
The transition between hidden states encodes truthfulness information.
papers.limitation:
Do not differentiate between fine-grained categories of hallucination.
Do not examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers, only the final layer.
Experiments are performed on conventional QA tasks, not more complicated or domain-specific tasks.
Future research is needed to develop more effective strategies for mitigating LLM hallucination.
future_direction: Explore different types of hallucination (factual fabrication, instruction inconsistency, etc.).
Examine hidden states in intermediate transformer layers and investigate layer-by-layer formation of hallucination.
Adapt the experimental framework to more complicated or domain-specific tasks and potentially extend to multimodal features.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can make up answers that are not real, and this is known as hallucination. This research aims to see if, how, and to what extent LLMs are aware of hallucination. More specifically, we check whether and how an LLM reacts differently in its hidden states when it answers a question right versus when it hallucinates. To do this, we introduce an experimental framework which allows examining LLM's hidden states in different hallucination situations. Building upon this framework, we conduct a series of experiments with language models in the LLaMA family (Touvron et al., 2023). Our empirical findings suggest that LLMs react differently when processing a genuine response versus a fabricated one. We then apply various model interpretation techniques to help understand and explain the findings better. Moreover, informed by the empirical observations, we show great potential of using the guidance derived from LLM's hidden representation space to mitigate hallucination. We believe this work provides insights into how LLMs produce hallucinated answers and how to make them occur less often.

papers.title: Illusion or Algorithm? Investigating Memorization, Emergence, and Symbolic Processing in In-Context Learning
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the extent to which in-context learning (ICL) in language models reflects true generalization versus memorization, and how ICL abilities and mechanisms develop during pre-training.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that in-context learning (ICL) is not purely memorization nor purely symbolic algorithmic processing, and reveals predictable development patterns for complex ICL tasks linked to internal subspace allocation in the residual stream.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that ICL is a mix of generalization and memorization, with predictable development for complex tasks, and internal mechanistic analysis reveals consistent subspace allocation patterns that advance understanding of ICL.
papers.key_findings:
LMs can perform pattern-based ICL tasks with random tokens, indicating generalization beyond memorization, but performance declines with rarer tokens, contradicting a pure symbolic algorithm view.
Different aspects of ICL develop idiosyncratically with model scale and training time, with performance gaps due to task configuration persisting while token frequency gaps stabilize.
The dimensionality of the residual stream subspace used for ICL follows a consistent pattern: an initial rise then decay, and development correlates with using a common subspace across tasks.
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited by the availability of fine-grained checkpoints, particularly between steps 512 and 1000 in Pythia training, which could provide further insights.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more fine-grained checkpoint intervals.
Applying the SUDA method to a wider range of tasks in interpretability.
Systematic investigation across diverse factual and reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Large-scale Transformer language models (LMs) trained solely on next-token prediction with web-scale data can solve a wide range of tasks after seeing just a few examples. The mechanism behind this capability, known as in-context learning (ICL), remains both controversial and poorly understood. Some studies argue that it is merely the result of memorizing vast amounts of data, while others contend that it reflects a fundamental, symbolic algorithmic development in LMs. In this work, we introduce a suite of investigative tasks and a novel method to systematically investigate ICL by leveraging the full Pythia scaling suite, including interim checkpoints that capture progressively larger amount of training data. By carefully exploring ICL performance on downstream tasks and simultaneously conducting a mechanistic analysis of the residual stream's subspace, we demonstrate that ICL extends beyond mere "memorization" of the training corpus, yet does not amount to the implementation of an independent symbolic algorithm. Our results also clarify several aspects of ICL, including the influence of training dynamics, model capabilities, and elements of mechanistic interpretability. Overall, our work advances the understanding of ICL and its implications, offering model developers insights into potential improvements and providing AI security practitioners with a basis for more informed guidelines.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: HACK: Hallucinations Along Certainty and Knowledge Axes
papers.research_question: How can hallucinations in large language models be categorized based on the model's internal properties (knowledge and certainty) rather than external properties, and how can this categorization inform targeted mitigation strategies?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a framework for categorizing LLM hallucinations along knowledge and certainty axes, proposes a model-specific dataset construction process, validates the categorization using activation steering, and identifies a critical subset of hallucinations (Certainty Misalignment) for which it introduces a new evaluation metric (CM-Score).
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination's underlying factors.
papers.key_findings:
Hallucinations can be systematically categorized based on whether the model possesses the correct parametric knowledge (HK+ vs HK-) and its certainty (HC+ vs HC-).
Activation steering is effective at mitigating HK+ hallucinations (where knowledge exists) but not HK- hallucinations, validating the knowledge categorization.
A significant subset of hallucinations (9%–43%) are Certainty Misalignment (CM) cases, where the model hallucinates with high certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally.
Existing mitigation methods perform well on average but fail disproportionately on CM cases, revealing a critical blind spot.
Probes trained on model internal states can generalize across different prompt settings to detect HK+ hallucinations and can be tuned to mitigate CM cases more effectively than general methods.
papers.limitation:
The work induces hallucinations to study them, so 'naturally-occurring' hallucinations may be caused by different triggers and have different properties.
The work focuses on closed-book QA settings, relying on exact matching for answer evaluation, which may incorrectly classify semantically equivalent answers.
Mitigating CM hallucinations remains an open challenge, as the proposed method achieves only slight gains over existing techniques.
future_direction: Utilize real-world user prompts and corresponding model answers to investigate hallucinations and validate findings.
Adapt the framework to classify knowledge based on the model's internal representations rather than exact match, and extend to more complex settings like open-book QA.
Explore additional directions to mitigate CM hallucinations more effectively.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in LLMs present a critical barrier to their reliable usage. Existing research usually categorizes hallucination by their external properties rather than by the LLMs' underlying internal properties. This external focus overlooks that hallucinations may require tailored mitigation strategies based on their underlying mechanism. We propose a framework for categorizing hallucinations along two axes: knowledge and certainty. Since parametric knowledge and certainty may vary across models, our categorization method involves a model-specific dataset construction process that differentiates between those types of hallucinations. Along the knowledge axis, we distinguish between hallucinations caused by a lack of knowledge and those occurring despite the model having the knowledge of the correct response. To validate our framework along the knowledge axis, we apply steering mitigation, which relies on the existence of parametric knowledge to manipulate model activations. This addresses the lack of existing methods to validate knowledge categorization by showing a significant difference between the two hallucination types. We further analyze the distinct knowledge and hallucination patterns between models, showing that different hallucinations do occur despite shared parametric knowledge. Turning to the certainty axis, we identify a particularly concerning subset of hallucinations where models hallucinate with certainty despite having the correct knowledge internally. We introduce a new evaluation metric to measure the effectiveness of mitigation methods on this subset, revealing that while some methods perform well on average, they fail disproportionately on these critical cases. Our findings highlight the importance of considering both knowledge and certainty in hallucination analysis and call for targeted mitigation approaches that consider the hallucination underlying factors.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
