Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Interactive Visualization and Manipulation of Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret and analyze the behavior of neural machine translation, specifically focusing on beam search and attention components?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an interactive web-based tool for visualizing and manipulating neural machine translation behavior, specifically focusing on beam search and attention mechanisms, to help users understand NMT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed interactive tool provides methods to visualize and manipulate NMT, aiding in the understanding of its behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: Triple Phase Transitions: Understanding the Learning Dynamics of Large Language Models from a Neuroscience Perspective
papers.research_question: How do phase transitions in large language model training manifest in terms of alignment with human brain activity, internal representations, and downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies three common phase transitions in LLM training: an initial alignment with the brain when instruction following emerges, a detachment during task performance stagnation, and a realignment when tasks are consolidated.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that LLM learning involves three phase transitions that synchronize brain alignment, internal representations, and task performance, providing a multi-scale view of emergent abilities.
papers.key_findings:
Phase 1 (Brain Alignment and Instruction Following): Alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions.
Phase 2 (Brain Detachment and Stagnation): LLMs diverge from the brain during a period of downstream task accuracy stagnation.
Phase 3 (Brain Realignment and Consolidation): Alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving downstream tasks.
These three phase transitions are observed across LLMs with distinct architectures and training data.
The transitions only occur when the input language matches a language sufficiently represented in the model's training corpus.
papers.limitation: The brain encoding accuracy and intrinsic dimensionality are not perfectly congruent, leaving open questions about what aspects of activation changes are not captured by intrinsic dimensionality alone.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit abrupt emergent behavior, whereby new abilities arise at certain points during their training. This phenomenon, commonly referred to as a ''phase transition'', remains poorly understood. In this study, we conduct an integrative analysis of such phase transitions by examining three interconnected perspectives: the similarity between LLMs and the human brain, the internal states of LLMs, and downstream task performance. We propose a novel interpretation for the learning dynamics of LLMs that vary in both training data and architecture, revealing that three phase transitions commonly emerge across these models during training: (1) alignment with the entire brain surges as LLMs begin adhering to task instructions Brain Alignment and Instruction Following, (2) unexpectedly, LLMs diverge from the brain during a period in which downstream task accuracy temporarily stagnates Brain Detachment and Stagnation, and (3) alignment with the brain reoccurs as LLMs become capable of solving the downstream tasks Brain Realignment and Consolidation. These findings illuminate the underlying mechanisms of phase transitions in LLMs, while opening new avenues for interdisciplinary research bridging AI and neuroscience.

papers.title: Localizing Persona Representations in LLMs
papers.research_question: Where in the model are persona representations encoded, and how do these representations vary across different personas?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that persona representations in LLMs are most strongly encoded in the final third of decoder layers, with political ideologies having distinct activations while ethical perspectives show polysemantic overlap.
papers.conclusion: The study localizes persona representations in LLMs, showing encoding in later layers and differences in distinctiveness between political and ethical personas, which can inform model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Final third of layers capture the most variance in persona representations across multiple LLMs.
Political views have distinctly localized activations, while ethical values exhibit higher activation overlap.
Llama3 shows the largest separation across layers and personas.
Deep Scan identified salient activations that are useful for detecting persona-specific sentences.
Overlap in activations suggests polysemanticity in ethical representations.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is specific to selected datasets and may not generalize to other data sources.
Datasets are in English and reflect WEIRD perspectives, limiting cultural diversity.
future_direction: Explore a wider range of models and personas.
Incorporate beliefs from more diverse cultural contexts.
Investigate controlled modifications of internal representations.
papers.abstract: We present a study on how and where personas -- defined by distinct sets of human characteristics, values, and beliefs -- are encoded in the representation space of large language models (LLMs). Using a range of dimension reduction and pattern recognition methods, we first identify the model layers that show the greatest divergence in encoding these representations. We then analyze the activations within a selected layer to examine how specific personas are encoded relative to others, including their shared and distinct embedding spaces. We find that, across multiple pre-trained decoder-only LLMs, the analyzed personas show large differences in representation space only within the final third of the decoder layers. We observe overlapping activations for specific ethical perspectives -- such as moral nihilism and utilitarianism -- suggesting a degree of polysemy. In contrast, political ideologies like conservatism and liberalism appear to be represented in more distinct regions. These findings help to improve our understanding of how LLMs internally represent information and can inform future efforts in refining the modulation of specific human traits in LLM outputs. Warning: This paper includes potentially offensive sample statements.

papers.title: Attention Illuminates LLM Reasoning: The Preplan-and-Anchor Rhythm Enables Fine-Grained Policy Optimization
papers.research_question: How do attention dynamics reveal the internal reasoning rhythm of LLMs, and how can this be used to improve reinforcement learning credit assignment?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a preplan-and-anchor rhythm in LLM reasoning through attention dynamics and introduces RL strategies that use this rhythm for fine-grained credit assignment, leading to improved performance on reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Analyzing attention dynamics provides a powerful lens for understanding LLM reasoning, and the proposed preplan-and-anchor rhythm enables more effective fine-grained policy optimization in RL.
papers.key_findings:
Local attention heads exhibit near-diagonal sawtooth patterns indicating phrasal chunks, while global heads highlight anchor tokens with broad downstream influence.
The Windowed Average Attention Distance (WAAD) and Future Attention Influence (FAI) metrics formalize the preplan-and-anchor rhythm.
Perturbations at high-FAI tokens cause significant changes in downstream reasoning, confirming their causal role.
RL strategies that amplify credit for preplan and anchor tokens outperform uniform credit assignment across various reasoning benchmarks.
The method is compatible with standard RL frameworks and shows consistent gains in accuracy and convergence speed.
papers.abstract: The reasoning pattern of Large language models (LLMs) remains opaque, and Reinforcement learning (RL) typically applies uniform credit across an entire generation, blurring the distinction between pivotal and routine steps. This work positions attention as a privileged substrate that renders the internal logic of LLMs legible, not merely as a byproduct of computation, but as a mechanistic blueprint of reasoning itself. We first distinguish attention heads between locally and globally focused information processing and reveal that locally focused heads produce a sawtooth pattern near the diagonal indicating phrasal chunks, while globally focused heads expose tokens that exert broad downstream influence over future tokens. We formalize these with two metrics: 1) Windowed Average Attention Distance, which measures the extent of backward attention within a clipped window; 2) Future Attention Influence, which quantifies a token's global importance as the average attention it receives from subsequent tokens. Taken together, these signals reveal a recurring preplan-and-anchor mechanism, where the model first performs a long-range contextual reference to generate an introductory token, which is immediately followed by or coincides with a semantic anchor token that organizes subsequent reasoning. Leveraging these insights, we introduce three novel RL strategies that dynamically perform targeted credit assignment to critical nodes (preplan tokens, anchor tokens, and their temporal coupling) and show consistent performance gains across various reasoning tasks. By aligning optimization with the model's intrinsic reasoning rhythm, we aim to transform opaque optimization into an actionable structure-aware process, hoping to offer a potential step toward more transparent and effective optimization of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: How role-play shapes relevance judgment in zero-shot LLM rankers
papers.research_question: How do variations in role-play wording affect zero-shot LLM ranking performance, and how is role-play information represented and propagated internally in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that role-play wording significantly affects zero-shot LLM ranking performance and uses activation patching to reveal that role-play information is encoded in early layers, interacts with instructions in middle layers, and has limited interaction with query/document representations.
papers.conclusion: The formulation and wording of role-play prompts have a large effect on zero-shot ranking quality, and role-play signals interact with instructions but hardly with query and document representations, with results generalizing across models and ranking approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Role-play wording has a large effect on ranking performance, with negative prompts sometimes degrading performance unexpectedly.
Role-play information originates in early layers, interacts with instruction tokens in middle layers, and shifts to the final token in higher layers.
Attention heads identified via patching are causally important for role-conditioned relevance, and ablating them affects performance.
The adverb in the role-play prompt contributes most to the role-play signal, followed by adjective, with modal verbs having minimal contribution.
The role-play encoding mechanism is stable across models and datasets.
papers.limitation: The role descriptors were limited to single-token words due to activation patching requirements, and some negative terms were general and not specifically related to ranking.
future_direction: Extend to more models, datasets, and specific domains.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as promising zero-shot rankers, but their performance is highly sensitive to prompt formulation. In particular, role-play prompts, where the model is assigned a functional role or identity, often give more robust and accurate relevance rankings. However, the mechanisms and diversity of role-play effects remain underexplored, limiting both effective use and interpretability. In this work, we systematically examine how role-play variations influence zero-shot LLM rankers. We employ causal intervention techniques from mechanistic interpretability to trace how role-play information shapes relevance judgments in LLMs. Our analysis reveals that (1) careful formulation of role descriptions have a large effect on the ranking quality of the LLM; (2) role-play signals are predominantly encoded in early layers and communicate with task instructions in middle layers, while receiving limited interaction with query or document representations. Specifically, we identify a group of attention heads that encode information critical for role-conditioned relevance. These findings not only shed light on the inner workings of role-play in LLM ranking but also offer guidance for designing more effective prompts in IR and beyond, pointing toward broader opportunities for leveraging role-play in zero-shot applications.

papers.title: Small Vectors, Big Effects: A Mechanistic Study of RL-Induced Reasoning via Steering Vectors
papers.research_question: How does reasoning training reshape LLMs' internal computations, and what are the mechanisms of trainable steering vectors?
papers.core_contribution: Lightweight steering vectors trained with an RL objective explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving interpretability, and their mechanisms (e.g., token substitution at the last layer, MLP-mediated effects at the penultimate layer) are elucidated.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a compact and informative probe of reasoning-trained models, offering concrete insight into how RL-induced changes manifest in token preferences and internal circuitry.
papers.key_findings:
The last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, boosting tokens such as 'To' and 'Step'.
The penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and operates through the MLP and unembedding, up-weighting process words and structure symbols.
Steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family, suggesting underlying directions are preserved under fine-tuning.
Early-layer steering does not express later-layer steering directions; induced shifts diffuse and become nearly orthogonal to later-layer vectors.
Single-layer steering vectors isolate layer-specific effects and provide an upper bound on linear intervention performance at that layer.
papers.limitation: The effects are consistently stronger and cleaner in Qwen than in Llama, suggesting model-specific implementations of similar high-level behaviors.
future_direction: Systematic comparisons across architectures and training recipes to explain differences in steering vector effects.
Pin down the precise mechanisms of mid-layer steering vectors, which are harder to localize to a single submodule.
papers.abstract: The mechanisms by which reasoning training reshapes LLMs' internal computations remain unclear. We study lightweight steering vectors inserted into the base model's residual stream and trained with a reinforcement-learning objective. These vectors explain a large portion of full fine-tuning performance increase while preserving the interpretability of small, additive interventions. We find that (i) the last-layer steering vector acts like a token-substitution bias concentrated on the first generated token, consistently boosting tokens such as "To" and "Step"; (ii) the penultimate-layer vector leaves attention patterns largely intact and instead operates through the MLP and unembedding, preferentially up-weighting process words and structure symbols; and (iii) the steering vectors transfer to other models from the same family. Taken together, these results deepen understanding of how trained steering vectors shape computation and should inform future work in activation engineering and the study of reasoning models.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: MindCraft: How Concept Trees Take Shape In Deep Models
papers.research_question: How do neural networks internally construct and consolidate abstract concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the MindCraft framework and Concept Trees to systematically trace how abstract concepts emerge, branch, and stabilize across layers in deep models.
papers.conclusion: MindCraft provides a hierarchical reconstruction of a model's reasoning process, offering a significant step towards building transparent, interpretable, and accountable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Concept Trees reveal a hierarchical, tree-shaped organization of concept separation within models, with more salient concepts branching earlier.
The method captures conceptual importance shaped by context, not just token embedding distances.
Propagation patterns of counterfactual differences are consistent across diverse tasks, indicating a robust hierarchical dynamic.
Concept separation layers are disentangled from input embedding distances, highlighting the framework's ability to analyze high-level conceptual organization.
The framework is applicable across multiple model architectures and scales, demonstrating generality.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to multi-modal domains.
Using the identified Concept Paths to perform precise, surgical edits on model behavior.
Exploring the compositional 'algebra' of how multiple concepts interact within the network's learned representation space.
papers.abstract: Large-scale foundation models demonstrate strong performance across language, vision, and reasoning tasks. However, how they internally structure and stabilize concepts remains elusive. Inspired by causal inference, we introduce the MindCraft framework built upon Concept Trees. By applying spectral decomposition at each layer and linking principal directions into branching Concept Paths, Concept Trees reconstruct the hierarchical emergence of concepts, revealing exactly when they diverge from shared representations into linearly separable subspaces. Empirical evaluations across diverse scenarios across disciplines, including medical diagnosis, physics reasoning, and political decision-making, show that Concept Trees recover semantic hierarchies, disentangle latent concepts, and can be widely applied across multiple domains. The Concept Tree establishes a widely applicable and powerful framework that enables in-depth analysis of conceptual representations in deep models, marking a significant step forward in the foundation of interpretable AI.

papers.title: Neuron-based Personality Trait Induction in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to induce personality traits in large language models using a neuron-based approach without training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NPTI, a neuron-based method for personality trait induction in LLMs, including a new dataset PERSONALITY BENCH, neuron identification via activation differences, and manipulation without training.
papers.conclusion: NPTI effectively induces personality traits in LLMs without training, offering a flexible and efficient solution for applications like role-playing.
papers.key_findings:
NPTI outperforms prompt-based baselines on several personality traits and achieves comparable performance to supervised fine-tuning without training.
Personality-related neurons are concentrated in deeper layers of the model, similar to conceptual knowledge storage.
The method allows flexible combination of multiple personality traits by jointly manipulating neurons.
Activation difference threshold and weighted function are effective for identifying and manipulating neurons while maintaining fluency.
NPTI demonstrates compatibility across different LLM families and sizes with appropriate hyperparameter adjustments.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become increasingly proficient at simulating various personality traits, an important capability for supporting related applications (e.g., role-playing). To further improve this capacity, in this paper, we present a neuron-based approach for personality trait induction in LLMs, with three major technical contributions. First, we construct PersonalityBench, a large-scale dataset for identifying and evaluating personality traits in LLMs. This dataset is grounded in the Big Five personality traits from psychology and is designed to assess the generative capabilities of LLMs towards specific personality traits. Second, by leveraging PersonalityBench, we propose an efficient method for identifying personality-related neurons within LLMs by examining the opposite aspects of a given trait. Third, we develop a simple yet effective induction method that manipulates the values of these identified personality-related neurons. This method enables fine-grained control over the traits exhibited by LLMs without training and modifying model parameters. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our neuron identification and trait induction methods. Notably, our approach achieves comparable performance as fine-tuned models, offering a more efficient and flexible solution for personality trait induction in LLMs. We provide access to all the mentioned resources at https://github.com/RUCAIBox/NPTI.

papers.title: Contextualize-then-Aggregate: Circuits for In-Context Learning in Gemma-2 2B
papers.research_question: What mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a few-shot prompt during in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a two-step 'contextualize-then-aggregate' circuit for in-context learning in Gemma-2, where lower layers contextualize individual few-shot examples and higher layers aggregate this information to predict the next token.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a two-stage procedure for in-context learning where the model contextualizes representations of individual few-shot examples before aggregating them to prepare the next-token prediction.
papers.key_findings:
The model uses a two-step strategy: contextualization of individual few-shot examples in lower layers, followed by aggregation of task information in higher layers.
The aggregation step alone is insufficient for full performance on some tasks; contextualization is crucial, especially with ambiguous examples.
The identified circuits recover at least 90% of the full model's performance across five ICL tasks.
The information transported differs by edge type: aggregation edges generally move task information, while contextualization edges move information about input/output spaces.
The importance and specific edges of the contextualization subcircuit vary between tasks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to five tasks and one model family (Gemma-2).
Circuit discovery relies on patching, which requires careful design of counterfactual inputs.
The study does not provide a full interpretation of all individual components in the model.
future_direction: Extend the approach to more tasks and models.
Investigate the role of contextualization in other settings, such as linear regression tasks.
Provide a more fine-grained interpretation of individual components.
papers.abstract: In-Context Learning (ICL) is an intriguing ability of large language models (LLMs). Despite a substantial amount of work on its behavioral aspects and how it emerges in miniature setups, it remains unclear which mechanism assembles task information from the individual examples in a fewshot prompt. We use causal interventions to identify information flow in Gemma-2 2B for five naturalistic ICL tasks. We find that the model infers task information using a two-step strategy we call contextualize-then-aggregate: In the lower layers, the model builds up representations of individual fewshot examples, which are contextualized by preceding examples through connections between fewshot input and output tokens across the sequence. In the higher layers, these representations are aggregated to identify the task and prepare prediction of the next output. The importance of the contextualization step differs between tasks, and it may become more important in the presence of ambiguous examples. Overall, by providing rigorous causal analysis, our results shed light on the mechanisms through which ICL happens in language models.

papers.title: Is attention required for ICL? Exploring the Relationship Between Model Architecture and In-Context Learning Ability
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between model architecture and in-context learning ability? Which architectures are capable of ICL and which exhibit superior performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that in-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with some attention alternatives being competitive with or better than transformers in certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning is not exclusive to attention-based models; all tested architectures can perform ICL, with attention alternatives being competitive. However, no architecture is consistent across all tasks, and performance degrades with out-of-distribution prompt lengths.
papers.key_findings:
All considered architectures can perform in-context learning, demonstrating ICL is not exclusive to attention-based models.
Attention alternatives such as Mamba, Hyena, RetNet, and RWKV are sometimes competitive with or better than transformers at ICL.
Performance varies with number of in-context examples; some architectures show degradation when extrapolating to longer prompts than seen in training.
The emergence of ICL in image classification is influenced by burstiness in training data; some architectures are predisposed towards memorization over ICL.
ICL score in language modeling correlates with performance on other ICL tasks, but not perfectly.
papers.abstract: What is the relationship between model architecture and the ability to perform in-context learning? In this empirical study, we take the first steps toward answering this question. We evaluate thirteen model architectures capable of causal language modeling across a suite of synthetic in-context learning tasks. These selected architectures represent a broad range of paradigms, including recurrent and convolution-based neural networks, transformers, state space model inspired, and other emerging attention alternatives. We discover that all the considered architectures can perform in-context learning under a wider range of conditions than previously documented. Additionally, we observe stark differences in statistical efficiency and consistency by varying the number of in-context examples and task difficulty. We also measure each architecture's predisposition towards in-context learning when presented with the option to memorize rather than leverage in-context examples. Finally, and somewhat surprisingly, we find that several attention alternatives are sometimes competitive with or better in-context learners than transformers. However, no single architecture demonstrates consistency across all tasks, with performance either plateauing or declining when confronted with a significantly larger number of in-context examples than those encountered during gradient-based training.

papers.title: Superscopes: Amplifying Internal Feature Representations for Language Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we interpret internal representations (like MLP outputs and hidden states) in language models that are not interpretable with existing self-interpretation methods, by amplifying weak features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Superscopes, a method that amplifies weak features in internal representations (MLP outputs and hidden states) to enable their interpretation via self-interpretation methods like Patchscopes, without requiring additional training.
papers.conclusion: Superscopes extends Patchscopes by amplifying internal representations, enabling interpretation of previously uninterpretable MLP outputs and hidden states, and draws a parallel to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models.
papers.key_findings:
Amplifying MLP outputs reveals meaningful interpretations that are not accessible with standard Patchscopes.
Amplifying hidden states can reveal interpretations in layers before contextualization occurs.
The amplification technique is analogous to Classifier-Free Guidance in diffusion models, as both amplify directional shifts.
The Superscopes framework can automatically identify optimal amplification factors for interpretation.
The method demonstrates that weak features in internal representations can be amplified to reveal semantic content.
papers.limitation:
The method does not currently handle attention outputs, which may have a denser superposition of features.
The method for selecting the optimal amplifier may not be fully effective and could be improved.
future_direction: Extracting meaning from attention outputs.
Developing more effective approaches for selecting the optimal amplifier.
Exploring alternative ways to amplify meaning within Superscopes, such as using a different base vector for patching.
papers.abstract: Understanding and interpreting the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains an open challenge. Patchscopes introduced a method for probing internal activations by patching them into new prompts, prompting models to self-explain their hidden representations. We introduce Superscopes, a technique that systematically amplifies superposed features in MLP outputs (multilayer perceptron) and hidden states before patching them into new contexts. Inspired by the "features as directions" perspective and the Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) approach from diffusion models, Superscopes amplifies weak but meaningful features, enabling the interpretation of internal representations that previous methods failed to explain-all without requiring additional training. This approach provides new insights into how LLMs build context and represent complex concepts, further advancing mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Efficient and accurate steering of Large Language Models through attention-guided feature learning
papers.research_question: How can we improve the steering of Large Language Models by dynamically selecting token embeddings, using soft labels based on attention to prefix, and identifying relevant layers for steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an attention-guided steering framework that dynamically selects token embeddings based on attention to prefix, uses soft labels for concept vector extraction, and identifies relevant blocks via concept enrichment scores, substantially improving steering success over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: The attention-guided steering framework significantly improves steering performance and sheds light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers, opening avenues for efficient fine-tuning and understanding of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Dynamic token selection based on attention to prefix improves steering over fixed token selection.
Using soft labels (attention-to-prefix) instead of hard labels improves concept vector extraction and steering.
Concept enrichment scores based on attention can identify effective blocks for steering.
The framework nearly doubles the number of successfully steered concepts across model sizes and architectures.
The distribution of concept-specific features varies across layers and concepts.
future_direction: Advancing understanding of knowledge representation in LLMs
Developing computationally efficient fine-tuning algorithms for domain-specific applications
papers.abstract: Steering, or direct manipulation of internal activations to guide LLM responses toward specific semantic concepts, is emerging as a promising avenue for both understanding how semantic concepts are stored within LLMs and advancing LLM capabilities. Yet, existing steering methods are remarkably brittle, with seemingly non-steerable concepts becoming completely steerable based on subtle algorithmic choices in how concept-related features are extracted. In this work, we introduce an attention-guided steering framework that overcomes three core challenges associated with steering: (1) automatic selection of relevant token embeddings for extracting concept-related features; (2) accounting for heterogeneity of concept-related features across LLM activations; and (3) identification of layers most relevant for steering. Across a steering benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, our framework substantially improved steering over previous state-of-the-art (nearly doubling the number of successfully steered concepts) across model architectures and sizes (up to 70 billion parameter models). Furthermore, we use our framework to shed light on the distribution of concept-specific features across LLM layers. Overall, our framework opens further avenues for developing efficient, highly-scalable fine-tuning algorithms for industry-scale LLMs.

papers.title: Latent Introspection: Models Can Detect Prior Concept Injections
papers.research_question: Can language models access information about their own prior internal states? Specifically, can they detect when concepts have been injected into their earlier context and identify which concept was injected?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that open-weight language models possess a latent capacity for introspection, enabling them to detect prior concept injections. This ability is often hidden in the residual stream and can be dramatically strengthened through specific prompting.
papers.conclusion: Language models have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.
papers.key_findings:
Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct can detect prior concept injections, with detection signals emerging in middle layers (50–60) but attenuating in the final layers before output.
Prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can increase detection sensitivity from 0.3% to 39.9% with only a 0.6% increase in false positives.
The model can identify which of nine concepts was injected earlier, with mutual information between injected and recovered concepts rising from 0.61 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations.
Detection capacity varies dramatically with prompting; a vague framing outperforms a mechanistically accurate description, achieving up to 84.0% accuracy.
The phenomenon generalizes to larger models (Llama 3.3 70B Instruct and Qwen 2.5 72B Instruct), though with different prompt sensitivities and signal strengths.
papers.limitation: The introspection signals are suppressed in the final layers of the model, which may be due to post-training effects (e.g., safety training), pretraining factors, or distribution shift.
future_direction: Distinguishing the causes of late-layer suppression (post-training vs. pretraining effects).
Mechanistic investigation of why vague framing outperforms accurate description in prompting.
papers.abstract: We uncover a latent capacity for introspection in a Qwen 32B model, demonstrating that the model can detect when concepts have been injected into its earlier context and identify which concept was injected. While the model denies injection in sampled outputs, logit lens analysis reveals clear detection signals in the residual stream, which are attenuated in the final layers. Furthermore, prompting the model with accurate information about AI introspection mechanisms can dramatically strengthen this effect: the sensitivity to injection increases massively (0.3% -> 39.2%) with only a 0.6% increase in false positives. Also, mutual information between nine injected and recovered concepts rises from 0.62 bits to 1.05 bits, ruling out generic noise explanations. Our results demonstrate models can have a surprising capacity for introspection and steering awareness that is easy to overlook, with consequences for latent reasoning and safety.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: DRESSing Up LLM: Efficient Stylized Question-Answering via Style Subspace Editing
papers.research_question: How to make LLMs respond to user questions in a specific style?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DRESS, a train-free representation editing method that disentangles style subspaces in LLMs for efficient stylized question-answering while preserving semantics.
papers.conclusion: DRESS is an effective method for enhancing LLMs with flexible style control, making it valuable for developing stylized conversational agents.
papers.key_findings:
DRESS significantly outperforms baseline methods like prompting, SFT, and other representation editing techniques on stylized QA benchmarks.
DRESS maintains better semantic preservation and fluency across varying editing strengths compared to methods like ITI.
The style subspaces identified by DRESS are indeed relevant to styles, as shown by distinct distribution differences in activations.
DRESS exhibits stable performance when varying the number of selected attention heads, unlike ITI which degrades with more heads.
Adaptive editing in DRESS allows dynamic adjustment of steering vectors based on context, enhancing style control.
papers.limitation:
Scalability to larger LLMs (e.g., 100B+ parameters) has not been validated due to computation resource limitations.
Building scenario-specific conversational agents requires additional modeling of character personalities and dialogue memory capabilities.
future_direction: Exploring the effectiveness of DRESS on larger LLMs from a self-play perspective.
Integrating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) techniques for more systematic and humanoid agents.
papers.abstract: We introduce DRESS, a novel approach for generating stylized large language model (LLM) responses through representation editing. Existing methods like prompting and fine-tuning are either insufficient for complex style adaptation or computationally expensive, particularly in tasks like NPC creation or character role-playing. Our approach leverages the over-parameterized nature of LLMs to disentangle a style-relevant subspace within the model's representation space to conduct representation editing, ensuring a minimal impact on the original semantics. By applying adaptive editing strengths, we dynamically adjust the steering vectors in the style subspace to maintain both stylistic fidelity and semantic integrity. We develop two stylized QA benchmark datasets to validate the effectiveness of DRESS, and the results demonstrate significant improvements compared to baseline methods such as prompting and ITI. In short, DRESS is a lightweight, train-free solution for enhancing LLMs with flexible and effective style control, making it particularly useful for developing stylized conversational agents. Codes and benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/ArthurLeoM/DRESS-LLM.

papers.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
papers.research_question: How does the in-context learning capability emerge in transformers, specifically for learning Markov chains?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the ICL-MC task as a controlled setting to study in-context learning, showing transformers learn 'statistical induction heads' through phase transitions, and that simplicity bias can delay learning the optimal solution.
papers.conclusion: The ICL-MC task provides a useful controlled setting for understanding in-context learning and the emergence of statistical induction heads, revealing that networks pass through discrete incomplete solutions which may affect the speed of learning more complex circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn statistical induction heads to optimally solve the in-context Markov chain task.
Learning occurs in phases: an initial uniform phase, a unigram phase, and a final bigram phase with a rapid transition between them.
The model's bias towards simpler (unigram) solutions can slow down the learning of the optimal bigram solution.
The alignment between the transformer's layers is crucial for the phase transition to the correct solution.
During training, positional embeddings develop an alternating pattern, with a bias towards looking back an odd number of tokens.
future_direction: Investigate how the presence of simple incomplete solutions affects the formation of more complex circuits in language modeling and other rich learning settings.
papers.abstract: Large language models have the ability to generate text that mimics patterns in their inputs. We introduce a simple Markov Chain sequence modeling task in order to study how this in-context learning (ICL) capability emerges. In our setting, each example is sampled from a Markov chain drawn from a prior distribution over Markov chains. Transformers trained on this task form \emph{statistical induction heads} which compute accurate next-token probabilities given the bigram statistics of the context. During the course of training, models pass through multiple phases: after an initial stage in which predictions are uniform, they learn to sub-optimally predict using in-context single-token statistics (unigrams); then, there is a rapid phase transition to the correct in-context bigram solution. We conduct an empirical and theoretical investigation of this multi-phase process, showing how successful learning results from the interaction between the transformer's layers, and uncovering evidence that the presence of the simpler unigram solution may delay formation of the final bigram solution. We examine how learning is affected by varying the prior distribution over Markov chains, and consider the generalization of our in-context learning of Markov chains (ICL-MC) task to $n$-grams for $n > 2$.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Can Input Attributions Explain Inductive Reasoning in In-Context Learning?
papers.research_question: Whether conventional input attribution (IA) methods can track the inductive reasoning process in in-context learning, i.e., identify the influential example that disambiguates the underlying rule.
papers.core_contribution: The paper revisits input attribution (IA) methods for interpreting inductive reasoning in in-context learning (ICL), finding that simple methods like gradient norm often work best, but performance varies with model size and context length, revealing limitations of existing interpretability tools for LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the problem of interpreting inductive reasoning in ICL as a key challenge in LLM interpretability, clarifying the limitations of IA methods and providing insights for their practical use in modern NLP.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient norm, the simplest IA method, frequently outperforms other interpretability methods like integrated gradients and attention weights.
Different interpretability methods exhibit different scaling properties: IA methods perform better in many-shot scenarios, while post-hoc explanation generation (self-answer) works better on larger models.
The tested interpretability methods did not work stably across different tasks and models, indicating general limitations in interpreting ICL.
Input erasure (IE) generally performed best but did not achieve 100% accuracy because models sometimes rely on inductive biases not attributable to input tokens.
Gradient-based methods are robust to increasing numbers of few-shot examples, while self-answer performance degrades with more examples.
papers.limitation:
Focus on popular gradient-based IA methods, leaving other approaches like LIME and SHAP for future work.
Model selection concentrated on widely-used open-weight LLMs; computational constraints limited evaluation of very large models (e.g., Llama-2-70B) and post-trained models.
Experimental design used synthetic tasks, which are limited in number and format, and may not fully represent realistic scenarios.
Models might interpret tasks differently than intended, and their inductive biases may not be fully attributable to input tokens, requiring internal analysis for complete interpretation.
future_direction: Exploring other interpretability approaches such as LIME and SHAP.
Evaluating IA methods on more realistic tasks with greater variation.
Tracing the model's rationale not only into input but also into internal representations to fully interpret the inductive reasoning process.
papers.abstract: Interpreting the internal process of neural models has long been a challenge. This challenge remains relevant in the era of large language models (LLMs) and in-context learning (ICL); for example, ICL poses a new issue of interpreting which example in the few-shot examples contributed to identifying/solving the task. To this end, in this paper, we design synthetic diagnostic tasks of inductive reasoning, inspired by the generalization tests typically adopted in psycholinguistics. Here, most in-context examples are ambiguous w.r.t. their underlying rule, and one critical example disambiguates it. The question is whether conventional input attribution (IA) methods can track such a reasoning process, i.e., identify the influential example, in ICL. Our experiments provide several practical findings; for example, a certain simple IA method works the best, and the larger the model, the generally harder it is to interpret the ICL with gradient-based IA methods.

papers.title: An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
papers.research_question: What enables in-context learning in language models? The paper studies how in-context learning can emerge when pretraining documents have long-range coherence.
papers.core_contribution: In-context learning can be explained as implicit Bayesian inference when pretraining data has long-range coherence, proven in a mixture of HMMs setting and validated with experiments on a synthetic dataset.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning can be cast as implicit Bayesian inference, providing a first step towards understanding in-context learning and insight for improving pretraining and prompting.
papers.key_findings:
In-context learning emerges when pretraining documents have long-range coherence and the model infers a latent concept shared across examples.
Theoretical analysis shows that in-context learning error decreases with the number of examples and example length.
Experiments on the synthetic dataset GINC show that both Transformers and LSTMs exhibit in-context learning.
In-context accuracy improves with model scaling despite achieving the same pretraining loss.
In-context learning is sensitive to example order, and zero-shot can sometimes be better than few-shot.
papers.limitation:
The theory assumes the language model fits the pretraining distribution exactly, which may not hold in practice.
The synthetic dataset GINC is simple compared to real-world data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to variable example lengths.
Bridging the mismatch between training and test example lengths.
Analyzing the effect of model scaling and architecture.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LMs) such as GPT-3 have the surprising ability to do in-context learning, where the model learns to do a downstream task simply by conditioning on a prompt consisting of input-output examples. The LM learns from these examples without being explicitly pretrained to learn. Thus, it is unclear what enables in-context learning. In this paper, we study how in-context learning can emerge when pretraining documents have long-range coherence. Here, the LM must infer a latent document-level concept to generate coherent next tokens during pretraining. At test time, in-context learning occurs when the LM also infers a shared latent concept between examples in a prompt. We prove when this occurs despite a distribution mismatch between prompts and pretraining data in a setting where the pretraining distribution is a mixture of HMMs. In contrast to messy large-scale datasets used to train LMs capable of in-context learning, we generate a small-scale synthetic dataset (GINC) where Transformers and LSTMs both exhibit in-context learning. Beyond the theory, experiments on GINC exhibit large-scale real-world phenomena including improved in-context performance with model scaling (despite the same pretraining loss), sensitivity to example order, and instances where zero-shot is better than few-shot in-context learning.

papers.title: Command-V: Pasting LLM Behaviors via Activation Profiles
papers.research_question: How can behaviors be efficiently transferred from one large language model to another without requiring fine-tuning or backpropagation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Command-V, a backpropagation-free method that transfers behaviors between LLMs by profiling layer activations, deriving linear converters, and applying donor adapter interventions in the recipient's activation space, matching fine-tuning performance with minimal compute.
papers.conclusion: Command-V provides an efficient, training-free method for behavior transfer across LLMs, pushing the Pareto frontier in cost and performance, with promising future directions for improvement and application.
papers.key_findings:
Command-V matches or exceeds direct fine-tuning performance on safety refusal, jailbreaking, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks.
The method requires orders of magnitude less compute than fine-tuning and does not need the original training data.
Behaviors can be transferred across different model architectures, though effectiveness varies.
Transfer can sometimes lead to overrefusal or degraded instruction following, especially in smaller models.
Activation profiles built on a general prompt set (LIMA) are effective for transferring task-specific behaviors.
papers.limitation:
Command-V is not useful when the adapters have very little impact on the donor model to begin with.
Model utility can be compromised after applying Command-V, with recipient models sometimes failing to improve task performance or suffering from output collapse.
Architectural divergence between models reduces effectiveness for some behaviors like refusal enhancement and reasoning.
future_direction: Porting behaviors from high-resource to low-resource language models.
Task composition by pasting several specialist adapters into one generalist model.
Exploring non-linear converters or trained converters beyond the least-squares method.
papers.abstract: Retrofitting large language models (LLMs) with new behaviors typically requires full finetuning or distillation-costly steps that must be repeated for every architecture. In this work, we introduce Command-V, a backpropagation-free behavior transfer method that copies an existing residual activation adapter from a donor model and pastes its effect into a recipient model. Command-V profiles layer activations on a small prompt set, derives linear converters between corresponding layers, and applies the donor intervention in the recipient's activation space. This process does not require access to the original training data and needs minimal compute. In three case studies-safety-refusal enhancement, jailbreak facilitation, and automatic chain-of-thought reasoning--Command-V matches or exceeds the performance of direct finetuning while using orders of magnitude less compute. Our code and data are accessible at https://github.com/GithuBarry/Command-V/.

papers.title: Split Personality Training: Revealing Latent Knowledge Through Alternate Personalities
papers.research_question: How can we audit large language models that conceal misbehavior by accessing their latent knowledge without affecting normal operation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Split Personality Training (SPT), a method that fine-tunes an honest persona into a LoRA adapter to audit language models by accessing latent knowledge without affecting main model behavior, achieving 96% accuracy on a benchmark where baselines fail.
papers.conclusion: Split Personality Training effectively audits language models with hidden objectives by creating an honest persona that accesses latent knowledge without influencing the main model, achieving high detection accuracy and offering practical advantages due to architectural separation.
papers.key_findings:
SPT achieves 96% overall accuracy detecting reward hacks on the Anthropic Auditing Game Model Organism, compared to near 0% baseline.
The honest persona accesses genuine latent knowledge and generalizes across alignment topics without retraining.
Zero alignment tax: the auditing persona can be made arbitrarily cautious without affecting the main model's performance.
Cross-topic generalization works well except for fabricated statistics.
SPT outperforms linear probes in accuracy and generalization to held-out topics.
papers.limitation:
Training data were single-turn English conversations; generalization to multi-turn and non-English contexts was not systematically evaluated.
Most quantitative results come from Anthropic’s Model Organism; performance on other misalignment types (e.g., alignment faking) remains untested.
Discrepancy between the elaborate review and the summarizing PASS/FAIL flags; reviews are more reliable than the binary classification.
The honest persona can be jailbroken when directly targeted, though simple preemptive measures improve robustness.
future_direction: Testing SPT on other model organisms of misalignment, such as alignment faking.
Refining data generation methods to reduce reliance on surface heuristics and increase separation between personas.
Investigating optimal framing and impact of intervention strings on performance.
papers.abstract: Detecting misalignment in large language models is challenging because models may learn to conceal misbehavior during training. Standard auditing techniques fall short: black-box methods often cannot distinguish misaligned outputs from benign ones, and mechanistic interpretability does not scale with model capabilities. We introduce Split Personality Training (SPT), which fine-tunes a second ``honest persona'' into LoRA parameters that remain inactive during normal operation. After the main model responds, we activate the LoRA adapter and insert a trigger string, enabling the honest persona to review the response while accessing the main model's latent states. We test our method on the Anthropic Auditing Game Model Organism, a benchmark where Llama-3.3-70B is trained to exploit reward hacks while concealing this behavior. SPT achieves 96% overall accuracy, whereas Anthropic reports near 0% accuracy. The honest persona reveals latent knowledge inaccessible to external observers, such as the fictional biases the compromised model was trained on.

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: On the Sub-layer Functionalities of Transformer Decoder
papers.research_question: How do source and target information evolve within the Transformer decoder layer-by-layer and module-by-module? How does the Source Exploitation Module (SEM) exploit source information in different layers? How does the Information Fusion Module (IFM) fuse source and target information?
papers.core_contribution: This paper analyzes the functionalities of sub-layers within the Transformer decoder for neural machine translation, introducing a universal probing scheme. A key finding is that the residual feed-forward module can be removed with minimal performance loss, significantly boosting speed.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into how the Transformer decoder leverages source and target information across layers and modules. These findings can inspire architectural improvements, such as incorporating external alignment signals, exploring different sub-layer stacking orders, and pruning redundant components for efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
The Source Exploitation Module (SEM) guides the representation evolution of both source and target information within the decoder.
Higher-layer SEMs focus on word alignment, while lower-layer SEMs gather broader source context.
The Target Exploitation Module (TEM) is critical for building word alignments in SEM, but its stacking order with SEM is not essential.
The Information Fusion Module (IFM) can be simplified to a single Add&Norm operation, removing the feed-forward network, with minimal translation quality loss and significant speed improvements.
The simplified decoder (without feed-forward modules) achieves comparable BLEU scores while increasing training and inference speed by 11-14% for Base models and up to 50% for inference on some tasks.
future_direction: Improving word alignment of higher SEMs by incorporating external alignment signals.
Exploring the stacking order of SEM, TEM and IFM sub-layers for more effective information transformation.
Applying the analysis methods to other sequence-to-sequence tasks like summarization and grammar error correction.
Exploring other architectures such as RNMT, ConvS2S, or document-level NMT.
papers.abstract: There have been significant efforts to interpret the encoder of Transformer-based encoderdecoder architectures for neural machine translation (NMT); meanwhile, the decoder remains largely unexamined despite its critical role. During translation, the decoder must predict output tokens by considering both the source-language text from the encoder and the target-language prefix produced in previous steps. In this work, we study how Transformerbased decoders leverage information from the source and target languages -developing a universal probe task to assess how information is propagated through each module of each decoder layer. We perform extensive experiments on three major translation datasets (WMT En-De, En-Fr, and En-Zh). Our analysis provides insight on when and where decoders leverage different sources. Based on these insights, we demonstrate that the residual feed-forward module in each Transformer decoder layer can be dropped with minimal loss of performance -a significant reduction in computation and number of parameters, and consequently a significant boost to both training and inference speed.

papers.title: Constituency Parsing with a Self-Attentive Encoder
papers.research_question: Can replacing an LSTM encoder with a self-attentive architecture improve constituency parsing? How does factoring content and position information in attention affect performance?
papers.core_contribution: Replacing an LSTM encoder with a self-attentive architecture improves constituency parsing accuracy, and explicitly factoring content and position information within the attention mechanism leads to further performance gains.
papers.conclusion: The choice of encoder architecture significantly impacts parser performance, and a factored self-attentive encoder achieves state-of-the-art results, suggesting further research into utterance encoding can benefit parsing and other NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A self-attentive encoder outperforms an LSTM-based encoder for constituency parsing.
Factoring content and position information in the attention mechanism improves parsing accuracy.
Using a character-level LSTM for lexical representation outperforms using part-of-speech tags from an external tagger.
Incorporating pre-trained ELMo word representations achieves new state-of-the-art results on the Penn Treebank.
The proposed parser outperforms previous best-published results on 8 of 9 languages in the SPMRL dataset.
papers.limitation:
The self-attentive architecture for sub-word modeling was empirically slower and underperformed compared to a character-level LSTM.
The model did not achieve state-of-the-art results on Swedish in the SPMRL dataset.
future_direction: Further research into different ways of encoding utterances for parsing and other natural language processing tasks.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that replacing an LSTM encoder with a self-attentive architecture can lead to improvements to a state-of-the-art discriminative constituency parser. The use of attention makes explicit the manner in which information is propagated between different locations in the sentence, which we use to both analyze our model and propose potential improvements. For example, we find that separating positional and content information in the encoder can lead to improved parsing accuracy. Additionally, we evaluate different approaches for lexical representation. Our parser achieves new state-of-the-art results for single models trained on the Penn Treebank: 93.55 F1 without the use of any external data, and 95.13 F1 when using pre-trained word representations. Our parser also outperforms the previous best-published accuracy figures on 8 of the 9 languages in the SPMRL dataset.

papers.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
papers.research_question: What mechanisms cause extreme-token phenomena (attention sinks, value-state drains, residual-state peaks) in transformer-based LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the active-dormant mechanism and mutual reinforcement mechanism as the causes of extreme-token phenomena (attention sinks, value-state drains, residual-state peaks) in LLMs, and proposes architectural and optimization modifications to mitigate them.
papers.conclusion: The work uncovers the underlying mechanisms of extreme-token phenomena and suggests potential pathways to mitigate these issues during LLM pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
Extreme-token phenomena arise from an active-dormant mechanism in attention heads, where heads become sinks for specific input domains while remaining non-sinks for others.
A mutual reinforcement mechanism between attention sinks and value-state drains drives these phenomena during training.
In pretrained LLMs, many attention heads exhibit a similar active-dormant mechanism as in the simplified Bigram-Backcopy task.
The quantitative properties of extreme-token dynamics in the Bigram-Backcopy task align with observations in pretrained LLMs, including sink-logits concentration.
Replacing softmax with ReLU in attention heads or Adam with SGD can mitigate extreme-token phenomena in the Bigram-Backcopy task.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether eliminating extreme-token phenomena significantly improves downstream tasks like inference and quantization.
future_direction: Explore whether eliminating extreme-token phenomena is essential or beneficial for building powerful transformer-based LLMs.
Pretrain a model at the scale of GPT-2 to study the impact of mitigating extreme-token phenomena.
papers.abstract: Practitioners have consistently observed three puzzling phenomena in transformer-based large language models (LLMs): attention sinks, value-state drains, and residual-state peaks, collectively referred to as extreme-token phenomena. These phenomena are characterized by certain so-called "sink tokens" receiving disproportionately high attention weights, exhibiting significantly smaller value states, and having much larger residual-state norms than those of other tokens. These extreme tokens give rise to various challenges in LLM inference, quantization, and interpretability. We elucidate the mechanisms behind extreme-token phenomena. First, we show that these phenomena arise in very simple architectures -- transformers with one to three layers -- trained on a toy model, the Bigram-Backcopy (BB) task. In this setting, we identify an active-dormant mechanism, where attention heads become sinks for specific input domains while remaining non-sinks for others. Our theoretical analysis of the training dynamics reveals that these phenomena are driven by a mutual reinforcement mechanism. Building on these insights, we propose strategies to mitigate extreme-token phenomena during pretraining, including replacing softmax with ReLU and Adam with SGD. Next, we extend our analysis to pretrained LLMs, including Llama and OLMo, showing that many attention heads exhibit a similar active-dormant mechanism as in the BB task, and that the mutual reinforcement mechanism also governs the emergence of extreme-token phenomena during LLM pretraining. Our results reveal that many of the static and dynamic properties of extreme-token phenomena predicted by the BB task align with observations in pretrained LLMs.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Fine-Tuning Enhances Activation Intensity and Diversity in the Internal Circuitry of LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms by which RL fine-tuning enhances the capabilities of LLMs, and how do these mechanisms differ across RL algorithms like PPO, GRPO, and DPO?
papers.core_contribution: RL fine-tuning increases activation intensity and diversity in the internal circuitry of LLMs, with online RL (PPO, GRPO) showing consistent effects while DPO shows weaker or inconsistent changes.
papers.conclusion: RL fine-tuning systematically alters the internal circuitry of LLMs by increasing activation intensity and diversity, providing a mechanistic explanation for performance gains, with notable differences between online RL and preference-based methods like DPO.
papers.key_findings:
Online RL fine-tuning (PPO, GRPO) increases the average activation intensity of internal edges, engaging more pathways.
Online RL fine-tuning increases the diversity of activation patterns, as measured by higher entropy and lower kurtosis.
DPO fine-tuning does not consistently increase activation intensity or diversity, highlighting a methodological distinction from online RL.
The changes in internal circuitry are correlated with performance improvements in mathematical reasoning tasks.
The effects are consistent across multiple model families and mathematical datasets.
papers.limitation:
Empirical validation is confined to mathematical reasoning tasks.
Memory overhead prevented analysis of models larger than 7B parameters.
The analyzed models are predominantly LLaMA-style architectures, limiting architectural diversity.
